name: Aeration
description: Mechanical introduction of atmospheric oxygen to oxidize dissolved gases, volatile compounds, and reduced multivalent metals.
chemistry_principle: Gas-liquid mass transfer according to Two-Film Theory. 4Fe(2+) + O2 + 10H2O -> 4Fe(OH)3(s) + 8H+. Increases dissolved oxygen to saturation and strips volatile CO2 and H2S.
suitable_applications: Groundwater with low DO, high ferrous iron (>0.3 mg/L), hydrogen sulfide odor, or excessive dissolved CO2 causing low pH.
prerequisites: Usually placed as the very first stage before coagulation or filtration to ensure oxidized precipitates can be trapped.
limitations: Ineffective for dissolved salts, heavy metal complexes, or nitrate; requires subsequent filtration to capture iron hydroxide flocs.
secondary_effects: Can strip CO2, driving pH slightly upward (typically +0.2 to +0.5 units).
reference: AWWA Water Quality and Treatment, 6th Edition, Ch. 5 (Gas Transfer)

name: Coagulation
description: Rapid chemical dispersion of multivalent metallic salts (alum, ferric chloride) to destabilize negatively charged colloidal suspensions.
chemistry_principle: Al3+ or Fe3+ hydrolyzes into positively charged polynuclear complexes (e.g. [Al13O4(OH)24(H2O)12]7+) that compress the electrical double layer and neutralize zeta potential (charge neutralization). Co-precipitates arsenate [HAsO4(2-)] onto ferric hydroxide matrices.
suitable_applications: Turbid surface water, river intake, colloidal clay, humic substances, and dissolved arsenate.
prerequisites: Rapid flash mixing (G > 700 s^-1) for 30-60 seconds; pH buffered between 6.0 and 7.8 for optimal alum hydrolysis.
limitations: Does not reduce dissolved salts (TDS), chloride, nitrate, or water hardness; generates chemical sludge.
secondary_effects: Consumes alkalinity (approximately 0.5 mg/L CaCO3 consumed per 1 mg/L alum added), lowering pH slightly.
reference: Letterman et al., AWWA Coagulation and Flocculation, 2011

name: Flocculation
description: Gentle, slow mechanical mixing to encourage destabilized colloidal particles to collide, agglomerate, and form heavy, settleable flocs.
chemistry_principle: Orthokinetic agglomeration governed by Smoluchowski collision kinetics: J = (4/3) * G * n1 * n2 * (r1 + r2)^3. Gentle velocity gradient (G = 20-70 s^-1) prevents shear breakage of delicate flocs.
suitable_applications: Directly downstream of rapid-mix coagulation prior to sedimentation.
prerequisites: Successful antecedent coagulation stage; gradual tapered mixing across 2-3 chambers (e.g., G = 50 -> 30 -> 15 s^-1).
limitations: Provides zero removal on its own without coagulation and subsequent gravity settling.
secondary_effects: Negligible chemical alteration beyond physical aggregate enlargement.
reference: Bratby, J., Coagulation and Flocculation in Water and Wastewater Treatment, 2016

name: Sedimentation
description: Quiescent gravity separation of aggregated floc particles from the clarified water stream.
chemistry_principle: Discrete and flocculent settling governed by Stokes' Law: vs = [g * (rho_p - rho_w) * d^2] / [18 * mu]. High density flocs settle into hopper sludge zones.
suitable_applications: High turbidity water following coagulation/flocculation; removes 80-90% of suspended solids burden prior to granular filters.
prerequisites: Requires formed flocs from preceding flocculation; overflow rate typically 1.5 - 2.5 m/h.
limitations: Ineffective for non-settleable microscopic colloids or dissolved ions; does not lower TDS.
secondary_effects: Sludge accumulation requiring regular hydraulic blowdown.
reference: Camp, T. R., Sedimentation and the Design of Settling Tanks, ASCE

name: Rapid Sand Filtration
description: Passage of clarified water through a granular media bed (graded quartz silica sand, anthracite) to capture residual suspended micro-flocs.
chemistry_principle: Deep-bed physical straining, hydrodynamic interception, sedimentation within pores, and van der Waals / electrostatic adhesion to grain surfaces.
suitable_applications: Standard clarification polishing to achieve drinking water turbidity < 1.0 NTU.
prerequisites: Pre-clarification (coagulation/sedimentation) for raw water with turbidity > 10 NTU to prevent premature bed blinding.
limitations: Does not remove dissolved minerals, heavy metal cations in solution, nitrate, or chloride.
secondary_effects: Requires periodic backwashing with treated water, generating backwash wastewater.
reference: Cleasby, J. L., Granular Bed and Precoat Filtration, AWWA

name: Ultrafiltration (UF)
description: Pressure-driven hollow-fiber membrane process with nominal pore sizes between 0.01 and 0.05 microns.
chemistry_principle: Size exclusion sieving mechanism: macromolecules, colloidal clays, bacteria, and protozoan cysts (Giardia, Cryptosporidium) are mechanically rejected by membrane pores.
suitable_applications: High-clarity membrane barrier for municipal surface water and critical RO pre-treatment (guarantees SDI < 2.5).
prerequisites: Pre-screening (100-300 micron strainer) to remove abrasive grit; coagulant addition may be utilized to reduce organic fouling.
limitations: Cannot reject dissolved monovalent/divalent salts, hardness, nitrate, or small organic molecules.
secondary_effects: Irreversible foulant accumulation over time requiring periodic chemical clean-in-place (CIP) with hypochlorite/citric acid.
reference: Cheryan, M., Ultrafiltration and Microfiltration Handbook

name: Granular Activated Carbon (GAC)
description: Fixed-bed adsorption through highly porous carbonaceous material offering surface areas up to 1000 - 1400 m2/g.
chemistry_principle: Physical adsorption via London dispersion forces and chemical sorption onto oxygenated surface functional groups (carboxylic, phenolic, lactonic). Traps hydrophobic synthetic organics, pesticides, taste/odor compounds, and chelates certain heavy metals.
suitable_applications: Removal of organic micropollutants, chlorine quench before RO, taste/odor control, and trace heavy metal polishing.
prerequisites: Turbidity must be < 1.0 NTU (particle-free) to prevent pore pore occlusion by suspended silt.
limitations: Does not soften water, reduce TDS, remove nitrate significantly, or lower chloride.
secondary_effects: Can support bacterial colonization (biological activated carbon), requiring post-disinfection.
reference: Sontheimer, H., Activated Carbon for Water Treatment, DVGW

name: Ion Exchange Softening / Demineralization
description: Reversible stoichiometric exchange of ions between aqueous solution and solid insoluble synthetic polymer resin beads.
chemistry_principle: Cation exchange: 2R-Na + Ca(2+) <-> R2-Ca + 2Na(+) and 2R-Na + Mg(2+) <-> R2-Mg + 2Na(+). Anion exchange (nitrate-selective): R-Cl + NO3(-) <-> R-NO3 + Cl(-). Selectivity driven by charge density: trivalent > divalent > monovalent.
suitable_applications: Targeted water softening (calcium/magnesium removal), nitrate-specific remediation, and heavy metal capture.
prerequisites: Pre-filtration (turbidity < 1 NTU) and removal of dissolved iron (<0.3 mg/L) to prevent irreversible resin fouling.
limitations: Softening replaces Ca/Mg with sodium ions (adding ~46 mg/L Na+ per 100 mg/L CaCO3 hardness removed). Resins exhaust and require regeneration with concentrated brine (NaCl).
secondary_effects: Increases sodium concentration in softened water; generates concentrated spent brine regenerant waste.

name: Lime-Soda Softening
description: Addition of hydrated lime [Ca(OH)2] and soda ash [Na2CO3] to raise pH and precipitate calcium as CaCO3(s) and magnesium as Mg(OH)2(s).
chemistry_principle: Carbonate hardness removal: Ca(HCO3)2 + Ca(OH)2 -> 2CaCO3(s) + 2H2O. Magnesium removal at pH ~10.8: Mg(2+) + 2OH(-) -> Mg(OH)2(s). Non-carbonate hardness removal: CaSO4 + Na2CO3 -> CaCO3(s) + Na2SO4.
suitable_applications: Large-scale municipal and industrial softening where extreme hardness (>300 mg/L) makes ion exchange brine disposal uneconomical.
prerequisites: Rapid chemical mixing, flocculation, heavy clarifier, and post-recarbonation (CO2 injection) to stabilize effluent pH.
limitations: Cannot soften water below solubility limits (~30-50 mg/L CaCO3); generates large volumes of caustic sludge.
secondary_effects: Significantly elevates pH (to 9.5 - 11.0), strictly necessitating downstream recarbonation / neutralization.
reference: AWWA Water Quality and Treatment, Ch. 13 (Chemical Softening)

name: Reverse Osmosis (RO)
description: High-pressure cross-flow membrane separation forcing water through a semi-permeable polyamide composite membrane against natural osmotic pressure.
chemistry_principle: Solution-diffusion transport: Water dissolves into the active thin-film polymer layer and diffuses across, while hydrated inorganic ions are repelled by electrostatic dielectric exclusion and size constraints (rejects 95-99% of ionic species).
suitable_applications: High TDS water (>500 mg/L), brackish groundwater, coastal chloride intrusion, simultaneous nitrate and heavy metal contamination.
prerequisites: Strict pre-treatment: Turbidity < 0.5 NTU (SDI < 3), dechlorination (free chlorine oxidizes polyamide), antiscalant dosing, and iron < 0.05 mg/L.
limitations: Energy-intensive (requires 10-65 bar feed pumps); generates 20-35% reject concentrate brine stream; produces demineralized low-pH aggressive permeate requiring remineralization.
secondary_effects: Rejects bicarbonate buffer, dropping permeate pH (often to 5.5 - 6.2); strips healthy essential minerals (calcium, magnesium).
reference: Malaeb, L., & Ayoub, G. M., Reverse osmosis technology for water treatment: State of the art review, Desalination

name: Chemical Precipitation (Heavy Metals)
description: Conversion of soluble heavy metal ions into insoluble hydroxides, sulfides, or carbonates by precise pH adjustment and precipitant addition.
chemistry_principle: Solubility product equilibrium (Ksp): Pb(2+) + 2OH(-) <-> Pb(OH)2(s) (Ksp ~ 1.4 x 10^-15 at pH 9.5-10.2). Ferric arsenate precipitation: Fe(3+) + H2AsO4(-) -> FeAsO4(s) + 2H(+).
suitable_applications: Groundwater or industrial runoff with elevated toxic heavy metals (Pb, Fe, As).
prerequisites: Coagulant aid / polymer addition followed by clarifier or microfiltration to trap micron-scale precipitate flocs.
limitations: Amphoteric metals (such as lead) re-dissolve at excessively high pH (>11.0); requires post-treatment pH neutralization.
reference: Patterson, J. W., Industrial Wastewater Treatment Technology

name: Neutralization / pH Adjustment
description: Controlled addition of acidic or alkaline chemicals to restore water to a neutral, non-corrosive, non-scaling pH range (6.8 - 7.8).
chemistry_principle: Acid-base neutralization: H(+) + OH(-) <-> H2O. For acidic water: addition of sodium hydroxide (NaOH), sodium carbonate (Na2CO3), or calcite (CaCO3) limestone contactors. For basic water: addition of carbon dioxide (CO2), hydrochloric acid (HCl), or sulfuric acid (H2SO4).
suitable_applications: Acidic raw water, post-RO permeate stabilization, recarbonation after lime softening, or pre-chlorination stabilization.
prerequisites: Continuous monitoring of pH and buffering alkalinity.
limitations: Only targets hydrogen ion activity; does not remove particulate matter, pathogens, or salinity.
secondary_effects: Alkaline adjustment with limestone slightly increases calcium hardness and TDS.
reference: Letterman, R. D., Water Quality and Treatment: A Handbook of Drinking Water Supplies

name: Biological Denitrification
description: Heterotrophic or autotrophic microbial reduction of nitrate under anoxic conditions to inert dinitrogen gas (N2).
chemistry_principle: Respiratory electron transport: NO3(-) -> NO2(-) -> NO -> N2O -> N2(g). Facultative bacteria (Pseudomonas, Paracoccus) utilize organic carbon (ethanol, acetic acid) as electron donor: 5CH3OH + 6NO3(-) -> 3N2 + 5CO2 + 7H2O + 6OH(-).
suitable_applications: Large-scale community groundwater treatment with excessive agricultural nitrate contamination where RO brine disposal is impractical.
prerequisites: Anoxic bioreactor, carbon electron donor dosing, followed by aeration, sand filtration, and robust disinfection.
limitations: Requires strict biological process control and temperature maintenance; introduces biomass risk into drinking water.
secondary_effects: Consumes dissolved oxygen, requiring subsequent re-aeration; introduces trace biomass requiring final filtration.
reference: Mateju, V., Biological Water Denitrification—A Review, Enzyme and Microbial Technology

name: Disinfection (Chlorination / UV)
description: Inactivation or destruction of pathogenic microorganisms (bacteria, viruses, parasites) via chemical oxidant (sodium hypochlorite) or UV radiation (254 nm).
chemistry_principle: Chlorination: Cl2 + H2O <-> HOCl + H(+) + Cl(-). Hypochlorous acid (HOCl) is ~80x more potent than hypochlorite ion (OCl-); penetrates microbial cell walls to denature enzymes. UV destroys thymine dimers in microbial DNA/RNA preventing replication.
suitable_applications: Mandatory final barrier for all potable water distribution systems to maintain residual bacteriostatic protection.
prerequisites: Turbidity must be < 1.0 NTU (ideally < 0.2 NTU) and low iron/organic content to prevent oxidant demand and pathogen shielding.
limitations: Does not remove dissolved chemical contaminants, heavy metals, or salinity; cryptosporidium oocysts show high chlorine resistance (UV preferred).
secondary_effects: Chlorination of waters containing dissolved natural organic matter (NOM) generates disinfection byproducts (trihalomethanes THMs, haloacetic acids HAAs).
reference: WHO Guidelines for Drinking-water Quality, Disinfection of Water Supplies
